scenes.tts: The first film showed growth slowing near carrying capacity. But when a crab count falls, did the population move, did carrying capacity move, or both? Return to the same creek. This time, follow a pair of trackers: teal for population size and gold for carrying capacity.
scenes.caption: The first film showed growth slowing near carrying capacity. But when a crab count falls, did the population move, did carrying capacity move, or both? Return to the same creek. This time, follow a pair of trackers: teal for population size and gold for carrying capacity.
scenes.visual: Open immediately on the exact schematic creek layout and colour map from the first film: teal crabs, gold food and capacity, green shelter, red challenges. Split one vertical gauge into a moving teal 'population now' marker and a gold 'supported over time' marker. Put the question between them while water and grass continue moving.
scenes.narration: The first film showed growth slowing near carrying capacity. But when a crab count falls, did the population move, did carrying capacity move, or both? Return to the same creek. This time, follow a pair of trackers: teal for population size and gold for carrying capacity.

scenes.visual: Keep both trackers moving gently over the dim creek. Brief title card: Did the Limit Move? Preserve every colour and object position from the hook.

scenes.tts: Population size means how many individuals are present now. Carrying capacity means the largest population the environment can support over time. The trackers can move together, but they are not the same measurement. A low population can sit below either a high or low capacity.
scenes.caption: Population size means how many individuals are present now. Carrying capacity means the largest population the environment can support over time. The trackers can move together, but they are not the same measurement. A low population can sit below either a high or low capacity.
scenes.visual: Enlarge the paired gauge to fill most of the frame. Move the teal marker among several levels while the gold marker holds, then move gold while teal holds. Beside it, transform one small creek panel between high-support and low-support states. Keep both cases labelled 'schematic'; do not imply a count reveals either state.
scenes.narration: Population size means how many individuals are present now. Carrying capacity means the largest population the environment can support over time. The trackers can move together, but they are not the same measurement. A low population can sit below either a high or low capacity.

scenes.tts: Begin with a brief cold event in this schematic creek. Some teal crabs disappear, so population size falls. Food, space, and shelter remain. Under that assumption, the gold support level stays put. The population may grow back toward it after the event passes.
scenes.caption: Begin with a brief cold event in this schematic creek. Some teal crabs disappear, so population size falls. Food, space, and shelter remain. Under that assumption, the gold support level stays put. The population may grow back toward it after the event passes.
scenes.visual: Lay a pale ice wash over the creek and remove some teal crab cartoons. Drop only the teal marker. Keep gold food dots circulating, green shelter swaying and the gold marker fixed. Remove the ice, then start a slow dotted teal recovery path toward gold. Label the case 'brief event; support assumed unchanged'.
scenes.narration: Begin with a brief cold event in this schematic creek. Some teal crabs disappear, so population size falls. Food, space, and shelter remain. Under that assumption, the gold support level stays put. The population may grow back toward it after the event passes.

scenes.tts: Now change the creek for the long term. Remove much of the green shelter and keep it gone. Young crabs have fewer hiding places, so in this model the environment supports fewer crabs over time. The gold carrying-capacity tracker moves down, and population growth now slows near that lower level.

scenes.visual: Reset to the neutral creek, then transform several green shelter clumps into bare shoreline and leave them absent. Reduce hiding spaces without changing the gold food dots. Slide the gold capacity marker downward. Compute a new schematic logistic curve that approaches the lower guide and label it 'computed model; habitat change schematic'.

scenes.tts: Here is the prediction. Both windows now show the same low crab count. The left followed a brief event. The right lost shelter for the long term. Can the count alone tell you whether carrying capacity moved? Hold your answer.
scenes.caption: Here is the prediction. Both windows now show the same low crab count. The left followed a brief event. The right lost shelter for the long term. Can the count alone tell you whether carrying capacity moved? Hold your answer.
scenes.visual: Place the brief-event creek and lasting-loss creek side by side with equal visible teal crab counts. Hide both gold markers behind question marks. Keep ice crystals drifting in the first window and bare shoreline in the second. Show only the question and neutral case labels; reveal no answer.
scenes.narration: Here is the prediction. Both windows now show the same low crab count. The left followed a brief event. The right lost shelter for the long term. Can the count alone tell you whether carrying capacity moved? Hold your answer.

scenes.visual: Deliberate thinking pause. Keep equal teal counts visible and gold markers hidden. Continue subtle water, ice and grass movement. Pulse the central question once without changing either case.

scenes.tts: No. The same abundance can come from different paths. To tell them apart, scientists need evidence about food, habitat, predators, weather, and survival across time. The count shows population size. It does not measure carrying capacity or identify which limiting factor caused a change.
scenes.caption: No. The same abundance can come from different paths. To tell them apart, scientists need evidence about food, habitat, predators, weather, and survival across time. The count shows population size. It does not measure carrying capacity or identify which limiting factor caused a change.
scenes.visual: Reveal the first gold marker unchanged and the second gold marker lower. Transform each question mark into a magnifying glass that scans existing food, shelter, predator, weather and survival symbols across a timeline. End on one equation-like statement made from labelled blocks: 'count = population size', while 'capacity' and 'cause' remain separate unknown blocks.
scenes.narration: No. The same abundance can come from different paths. To tell them apart, scientists need evidence about food, habitat, predators, weather, and survival across time. The count shows population size. It does not measure carrying capacity or identify which limiting factor caused a change.

scenes.tts: That matters for the winter dredge survey. Crews sample buried crabs across the Bay and build a Bay-wide estimate. The estimate is not an exact count. It can show whether reported groups rose or fell. By itself, it cannot show why they changed.
scenes.caption: That matters for the winter dredge survey. Crews sample buried crabs across the Bay and build a Bay-wide estimate. The estimate is not an exact count. It can show whether reported groups rose or fell. By itself, it cannot show why they changed.
scenes.visual: Transform the creek into a wide Bay map. Move a small dredge between scattered sample dots, lifting teal crab symbols from mud. Flow the samples into a large block labelled 'Bay-wide estimate'. Animate neutral up and down arrows for reported groups, but show no lesson-table values and no answer to its questions. Keep 'capacity?' and 'cause?' unresolved.
scenes.narration: That matters for the winter dredge survey. Crews sample buried crabs across the Bay and build a Bay-wide estimate. The estimate is not an exact count. It can show whether reported groups rose or fell. By itself, it cannot show why they changed.

scenes.tts: A lasting gain in food or shelter can raise environmental support. Lasting habitat loss can lower it. People can affect both trackers too. Harvest removes individuals, while shoreline building can remove marsh. Removing individuals does not automatically prove that the support level changed.

scenes.visual: Return to one creek and the paired gauge. Add green shelter and raise gold support; reverse the transformation and lower it. Then move a few teal crabs into a labelled harvest basket while gold stays neutral. Finally transform green marsh into built shoreline and lower gold. Mark all cases 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: Return to the paired trackers. A brief shock moved the teal population while gold support stayed. Lasting shelter loss moved the gold level too. Keep the distinction whenever a graph rises or falls. Ask what changed, how long it lasted, and what evidence measured it.

scenes.visual: Replay the two transformations rapidly in the same creek: brief ice lowers teal only; persistent shelter loss lowers gold too. Then transform the paired gauge into a generic rising-and-falling graph with three question labels: 'what changed?', 'how long?' and 'what evidence?'. Remove the labels one at a time before the end card.
